strategy.summary: Small, founder-owned Czech machine shop (60 staff), financially sound and fully booked with a backlog of more than six months. It has stopped taking new projects. We are a small customer to it (about 2.2% of its turnover). It holds 70% of part:320031 (Flange DN100) under a framework contract at a price far below the German second source. It is qualified on part:320030 with a 0% quota, where it quoted much higher than its 2025 bid. It is invited to the RFQ for the new HX shaft (part:320070). Delivery has collapsed, consistent with overload, and the share of late deliveries is worsening; quality improved but is still about twice the peer median. Leverage sits mostly with the supplier. What it values is a binding, plannable commitment and punctual payment, not volume as such. It has settled below its ask in every renewal on part:320031, but capacity now firms its stance. Evidence on the people involved is thin: no named contact and no call notes.
strategy.decision_maker: Most likely the founder/owner, as in a small s.r.o. with no visible approval ladder. No named contact exists in the records.

persona.style: courteous and relationship-minded (trade fair invitation), historically accommodating on renewals; now confident and selective because it is fully booked
other_traits: demands binding 12-month commitment for extra volume
underbid part:320030 in 2025 and is now recovering margin

needs.detail: It wants binding, plannable load before confirming extra volume and prefers longer, firm commitments.

It is not in distress, but we pay most invoices late against already short terms. Punctual payment is a low-cost goodwill item for us.
Bar steel and labour have risen. It may seek recovery on part:320031, which is priced well below the rival, and is already recovering margin on part:320030.

constraints.detail: Backlog of more than six months; no new projects. It may decline or quote high on the HX shaft, and short lead times would be priced steeply.
On-time delivery fell sharply year on year, below the 95% target and the peer median. We are a minor customer to it.
Prices on part:320031 are fixed per calendar year. Changes need 90 days' notice before year end. The contract auto-renews unless terminated with 90 days' notice.
Our only alternative on part:320031 (Lindlbauer) is far dearer, so moving volume away raises our own cost.

Caps part:320030: the quote sits above a no-margin German-plant cost, while its own plant is cheaper. Do not lean on it as the main lever, because a capacity-full supplier may dismiss it.
A cost-base-adjusted anchor for the new shaft. Confidence is low, so use it moderately.
A factual, checkable decline. Use it to secure delivery commitments, not as a threat.

Rising volume on part:320030 for a second-source role.

trades.why: It explicitly asks for binding volume. Commit our real need as binding in exchange for price and confirmed capacity.
Planning security for a full shop; 24 months captures the value.
Accept its own or a longer lead time to fit its schedule. This costs us little and is worth more than price to an overloaded shop.
The current term is already short against our standard. Do not ask for longer terms; offer punctual payment instead. Go shorter only as a last-round trade if it signals cash interest.
Secure a quality and delivery commitment while giving planning security.
Contract notice rules support a later start for any increase. Offer a later date at a slightly higher price.
Avoid a bar-steel clause while that index is near its high. Consider one only if it insists and the index trend is falling.

price_view.reasoning: Part:320031 is already well below the rival and the standard price, and was cut at the last renewal. Cost drivers point up, and there is no should-cost. The aim is to hold or limit any increase. Part:320030: the quote jumped versus 2025 far beyond what drivers explain and sits above the incumbent's price, so there is some room. Part:320070: no history; anchor on the adjusted should-cost, but a capacity-full supplier will price high or not quote.

Persona evidence is thin; adapt after the first reply.

findings.text: Part 320030 (flange DN65): Hrvelec's current quote EUR 16.33 [quote:7200009] sits +6.0% above our should-cost EUR 15.40 [cost:320030]. That should-cost has no margin, so the quote implies a thin margin. The cost model is built on the German plant of sup:70220, not Hrvelec's Czech plant; a CZ cost base would be lower, so Hrvelec's real margin is likely larger. Its 2025 quote was EUR 13.90 [quote:7100025]; the new quote is +17.5% on that. Material-weighted drivers explain only about +4.8% (bars +3.9%, labour +0.9%). Most of the jump is therefore margin or a reaction to its full order book. The incumbent sup:70220 supplies at EUR 16.02, below Hrvelec's quote.

Part 320031 (flange DN100): Hrvelec charges EUR 19.90 from 2026-01, after a -3.1% cut at renewal. That is 27% below the second source sup:70230 at EUR 25.34 and below the standard price of EUR 22.94. There is no should-cost for this part, so we cannot verify its margin. The price is already low, and driver moves (bars +12.3% x 0.29, labour +2.7% x 0.35, about +4.5%) argue for an increase rather than a cut. Room for a reduction is small; the realistic aim is to hold at 19.90.

Part 320070 (pump shaft HX, new part): our should-cost is EUR 36.87 on a German cost base, with confidence only 10%. Scaled to CZ (x0.82) it is about EUR 30.2 before margin. There is no price or quote history from Hrvelec, and RFQ 6000000305 is open. A fair target with margin is roughly EUR 33-35. Evidence is thin.

Cost drivers over 12 months mostly favour the supplier. Cold-drawn bars are +12.3%, though -2.3% off the June 2026 peak. Labour is +2.7%. Alloy surcharge 1.4404 is +5.9%, but -5.5% since 2026-06 and -13% below its 36-month peak. Electricity is -3.7%, which is immaterial at 1-5% weight. An increase of at most about 4-5% is defensible on 320030/320031, and about 3-4% on 320070. Since the June peaks, bars and alloy are easing, which argues against further rises.
Hrvelec has a habit of settling below its ask (average gap 2.6 pp). However, it is fully booked and requires binding 12-month commitments, which reduces its price flexibility now.

findings.text: Small founder-owned Czech machine shop (60 staff, EUR 2.81 M turnover, founded 1999). Decisions most likely sit with the founder/owner and there is probably no long approval ladder. The evidence names no person and holds no call or meeting notes, so the persona picture is thin.

Financially sound and stable: equity ratio 30.2%, credit index 246 and unchanged for 12 months, VDA 6.3 grade B. There is no sign of financial stress, so it can afford to walk away. Margin pressure is not a lever.

Capacity is the key fact. It has been fully booked since July 2026, with a backlog of more than six months, and it has stopped taking new projects. On 2026-09-24 it wrote that order intake is very strong and that it will confirm additional volume only against a binding 12-month commitment. It does not need our volume as such. What it values is a binding, long, plannable commitment. Expect a weak or high-priced reply to the HX shaft RFQ (part:320070, 4200 pc, SOP March 2027), or a refusal to quote.
We are a small customer to it: spend of about EUR 61.6k in FY2026 is about 2.2% of its turnover. Combined with the full order book, there is a real risk that it deprioritises our deliveries.

Delivery has degraded to 62.5% on time against requested dates (75% against its own confirmed dates), down from 84% a year earlier. The peers' median is 84.6% and the target is 95%. This is consistent with capacity overload. It weakens its position and is a supply-risk red flag. Quality improved to 980 ppm from 2300 ppm, with no overdue 8D reports, but is still about twice the peers' median.

Our payment behaviour is a sensitivity. We pay 88.1% of invoices late, on average 5.7 days late and at most 13 days, against already short 45-day terms. It can raise this, and offering on-time or faster payment is a cheap concession that gives it cash certainty.

The style is courteous and relationship-oriented: it invited us to its booth at the regional supplier fair. On 320031 its history is accommodating: it settled well below its ask in renewals and cut the price by 3.1% since 2023. Its price there is far below the second source Lindlbauer (EUR 25.34 vs 19.90), so it has little room to cut and could argue that the price is underpriced.

The frame contract runs to 2027-06-30 with prices fixed per calendar year. Price changes need 90 days' written notice before year end, and the renewal can be stopped by giving notice by 2027-04-01. This gives a planning window and a credible exit on parts where we own the tooling.

findings.text: Framework agreement covers only part:320031 (Flange DN 100). Prices are fixed per calendar year; any change needs written notice at least 90 days before year end, i.e. by 2026-10-02 for 2027. An increase notified later cannot take effect before 2028. Effective-date terms should anchor on 2027-01-01 at the earliest.
The term runs 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30 and auto-extends by 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice (by 2027-04-01). We keep a credible exit option, but the supplier can also give notice.

Commercial terms: payment 45 days net, shorter than our 60-day standard, so this is already a benefit to the supplier and gives us trade room. Delivery is FCA with a 42-day lead time, so we bear the freight. The quality agreement sets a 95% on-time target and a EUR 150 flat fee per supplier-caused complaint.

Renewal history on part:320031 is very favourable to us. They asked +2.4% and settled 0; asked +3.3% and settled 0; asked -1.0% and settled -3.1%. On average they settle about 2.6 pp below their ask, and the current price of EUR 19.90 is below the 2023 price of EUR 20.53. The sample is only three events on one part.

Price position on 320031: the supplier is far cheaper than the 30% second source Lindlbauer, which charges EUR 25.34 (+27%) and quoted EUR 27.00 in rfq:6000000112. We own the tooling, so the part can move, but moving would raise our cost. Citing the rival price would only help the supplier.

Mutual dependency is low on their side and moderate on ours. Our spend is about EUR 62k per year, roughly 2.2% of their EUR 2.81M turnover. They report being fully booked and ask for a binding 12-month commitment before confirming extra volume. Their finances are sound (equity 30%, credit index stable), so they can afford to walk away.

Performance is weak and gives us contract-based arguments. On-time delivery is 62.5% against the 95% contractual target, down from 84% a year earlier. Defects run at 980 ppm against a peer median of 457 ppm, though this improved from 2300 ppm. Our own payment behaviour is an exposure: on average we pay 5.7 days late.

For part:320030 the supplier is qualified but holds a 0% quota; sup:70220 holds 100% and we own the tooling (rfq:6000000209 second-source benchmark is quoted). For part:320070, a new stainless shaft, there is no sourcing yet and rfq:6000000305 is open. Should-cost for 320070 at the CZ cost base is about EUR 30.23. A full order book may limit their interest in both.

findings.text: Delivery is deteriorating sharply: rolling 12-month on-time against requested date fell from 95.2% (2024Q3) to 84% (2025Q3) and 62.5% (2026Q3); against its own confirmed date only 75%. 25% of receipts were late, averaging 11.7 days and up to 32 days. This is far below the 95% target in the quality agreement and below the 84.6% peer median. It is our strongest performance argument for price or terms, e.g. lead time or a ppm/OTD commitment.

Quality has improved but is still above peers: rolling ppm fell from 2309 (2025Q1) to 980 (2026Q3), with no overdue 8Ds. The peer median is 457 ppm. All 15 QNs are on part:320031, and 14 were supplier-caused. Recurring defects are wrong material certificate (3x), porosity, leakage and coating. Only EUR 150 flat is recharged per complaint, and several QNs were recharged 0. The supplier will point to the improving trend, so the quality argument is a supporting one only.

The supplier is very cheap on part:320031. It charges EUR 19.90 against EUR 25.34 at second source sup:70230, which holds a 30% quota and has better quality (0 ppm over the last 12 months). That price gap works for the supplier, so we should not cite the rival's price. Its price already fell 3.1% in 2026, and it historically settles below its ask.

Our volume outlook for part:320031 is flat: 4,420 forecast against 4,364 ordered in the last 12 months, so this is no growth lever. The new HX shaft part:320070 starts production in 2027-03 with about 2,390 pcs over the next 12 months and has no orders yet. That is the only real volume carrot. Part:320030 is currently bought from sup:70220, not from this supplier. Our spend is about 2.2% of the supplier's turnover, and it reports being fully booked, so our leverage through volume is weak.

Delivery history: there are 7 lines confirmed later than requested and 4 over-deliveries. The data has a known issue where requested and confirmed dates differ by 10-30 points. The confirmed-date OTD of 75% is the fairer figure to cite.

arguments.text: Flange DN100 (part:320031) is already by far your cheapest source: EUR 19.90 against EUR 25.34 at Lindlbauer, about 21% below. We cut 3.1% at the last renewal although we had offered only 1%. Any further cut would be unsustainable. Moving volume away costs you more than it costs us.

Our cost drivers rose while our price fell. Cold-drawn bar is up 12.3% in 12 months and is roughly 29% of the part's cost. Labour is up 2.7% and is about 35% of cost. Together that is about 4.5% of cost pressure against a 3.1% price cut. We asked 2.4% and 3.3% in earlier years and got 0 both times.

Capacity is scarce. We are fully booked for more than six months and have stopped taking new projects. Extra volume, shorter lead times or HX shaft capacity can only be granted against a binding 12-month commitment, and at a price that reflects this.

Quality has improved steadily. Quality complaints (QNs) fell from 7 to 3 per 12 months, and ppm fell from 2,300 to 980. There are no overdue 8D reports, and the last supplier-caused complaint was in February 2026.
You pay late. 88% of invoices are paid after the due date, on average 5.7 days late, against already moderate 45-day terms. Punctual payment, or a shorter term, is a fair counter-item.

On Flange DN65 (part:320030) our EUR 16.33 quote reflects today's bar prices, today's load and the larger volume of 15,600 pieces per year. Our 2025 bid of EUR 13.90 was made when we had free capacity.

weak_points: On-time delivery has collapsed to 62.5% against the requested date (75% against confirmed), versus the 95% target in the quality agreement. Lateness has worsened every quarter.
ppm of 980 is still about twice the peer median, and Lindlbauer is at 0 ppm.
Our DN65 quote jumped 17% versus 2025 and sits above the incumbent's EUR 16.02, which the drivers do not justify.
The DN100 price is fixed per calendar year. Any increase for 2027 needed written notice 90 days before year end, so by early October.
Hollerau is only about 2.2% of our turnover, so we look like we are deprioritising them.
Electric power prices are falling, and iron castings rose only 1.8%.
Hollerau already holds a 30% second source on DN100 and could shift share, even at higher cost.
wants: A binding 12-month or longer volume commitment, or a contract extension to 2028.
Smoothed, firm call-offs and a relaxed lead time, e.g. 56 days instead of 42.
Punctual payment, or 30 days instead of 45.
An index clause on bar steel instead of a fixed price.
A fair recovery on DN100 of roughly +3 to +4%, or at least price held.
No chargeback or ppm penalty increases.
red_lines: No price cut on DN100 below EUR 19.90.
No additional volume or HX shaft capacity without a binding commitment.
No lead time shorter than 42 days.
No punitive late-delivery or ppm penalties beyond the EUR 150 flat fee.
We will not accept work at a loss to win HX; we would rather decline.
red_team.opening: Thank Hollerau for the long cooperation and acknowledge openly that delivery reliability has slipped because we are fully booked. Point to the quality improvement. Then state that bar steel (+12.3%) and labour (+2.7%) rose while we cut the DN100 price by 3.1%. Propose +3.5% on DN100 from 1 January 2027, or the price held with a steel index clause. In exchange for a binding 12-month volume, a 2-year extension, punctual payment and a 56-day lead time, we would commit firm capacity, an on-time delivery recovery plan, and consideration of the HX shaft.

rebuttals.answer: We are not asking for a further cut. Our aim is to keep today's price, which is the price on our current orders, and to make the relationship more plannable for both of us. A competitive price only helps us if the parts arrive when we need them. That is why we want to talk about reliability and commitment, not only price.

Bar and labour costs did rise, and we take that seriously. We should keep it in proportion, though. Bar is only part of your cost, and it has eased from its recent peak. Power, a smaller item, has fallen. Weighted by their share of the part, the drivers support a modest adjustment, not a step change. Under our framework, prices are fixed per calendar year, and any change needs timely written notice. In past renewals we have always found a balanced result together, and we would like to do the same again.

We understand your order book is full, and we want to answer your request concretely. We can offer a binding commitment within our stable, shared forecast and a longer framework term. We can also accept your standard lead time rather than ask for shorter ones. In return we need confirmed capacity and deliveries on the confirmed dates, which have slipped clearly below the agreed target over the past year.

The rolling level is still well above the peer median, and there were supplier-caused complaints on this part during the year. We would welcome a ppm commitment that secures the progress you have made.
That is a fair point, and we accept it. We commit to paying on the agreed due date from now on, without asking you for longer terms in return.

We see that load and bar prices have changed since your earlier bid. Bar prices have eased recently, though, and the increase in your quote goes well beyond what the drivers explain. Our cost estimate for a German plant, with no margin included, is below your quote, and the larger volume should work in your favour. We see room to bring the quote closer to the market level.

press: We would value a joint recovery plan that brings on-time delivery back to the target in our quality agreement, and we are glad to align our call-offs to support it.
Would a ppm target close to the peer level fit with the quality progress your team has already made?
